analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָם אֶל לוֹט means “Abram said to Lot.” The name identifies Abram as the speaker.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew personal proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It is the subject of וַיֹּאמֶר.
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָם אֶל לוֹט, “Abram said to Lot,” אֶל introduces Lot as the person Abram addresses.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition without a prefix or suffix.

evidence.note: The genealogy lists Abram and Haran among Terah’s sons and names Lot as Haran’s son.
וְלוֹט עִמּוֹ names Lot as a companion of Abram on the journey from Egypt.

article.name: לוֹט
article.summary: Lot was the son of Haran, Abram’s brother. He accompanied Abram from Egypt toward the Negeb. The meaning of his name is uncertain.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for לוֹט. The derivation of the name is uncertain.
draft.definition: Lot, son of Haran and nephew of Abram.
draft.evidence: Genesis 11:27 names Haran as Lot’s father. Genesis 13:1 names Lot as Abram’s companion on the journey from Egypt.

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָם אֶל לוֹט, “Abram said to Lot,” אֶל marks Lot as the addressee. Abram appeals to their kinship when he says כִּי אֲנָשִׁים אַחִים אֲנָחְנוּ, “for we are kinsmen.”
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The preceding preposition אֶל is a separate word.

analysis.evidence: In אַל נָא תְהִי מְרִיבָה, נָא marks Abram’s plea, and מְרִיבָה is the subject of תְהִי. Abram asks Lot, “Please, let there be no quarrel between me and you.”
analysis.morphology: Hebrew negative particle with no prefix or suffix. It negates the third-person feminine singular jussive תְהִי.

analysis.evidence: In אַל נָא תְהִי מְרִיבָה, אַל negates the jussive תְהִי, and נָא softens Abram’s appeal to Lot: “Please let there be no quarrel between me and you.”
analysis.morphology: Hebrew particle of entreaty, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אַבְרָם asks לוֹט, אַל־נָא תְהִי מְרִיבָה, “Please let there be no strife.” The phrases beginning with בֵּין identify the parties between whom Abram asks that no strife exist.
analysis.morphology: Short Qal jussive, third person feminine singular, agreeing with the following subject מְרִיבָה.

analysis.evidence: מְרִיבָה is the subject of אַל־נָא תְהִי, “please let there be no strife.” Abram names the parties between whom he wants to prevent a quarrel, first himself and Lot, then their respective herders.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the absolute state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: וַיֹּאמֶר אַבְרָם אֶל לוֹט identifies Abram as the speaker and Lot as his addressee. In מְרִיבָה בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶיךָ, Abram asks that there be no strife between himself and Lot.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition with a first-person common singular pronominal suffix referring to Abram.
analysis.sense: between (two parties): of covenant, sign, witness, strife

analysis.evidence: Abram asks that there be no מְרִיבָה (“strife”) בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶיךָ (“between me and you”). The marked word identifies Lot as the second party to the potential dispute.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וּ means “and.” The preposition בֵּין takes the second-person masculine singular suffix ךָ, referring to Lot.
analysis.sense: between (two parties): of covenant, sign, witness, strife

analysis.evidence: In וּבֵין רֹעַי וּבֵין רֹעֶיךָ (‘and between my herders and yours’), the marked וּבֵין introduces Abram’s herders as the first of the two groups involved in the quarrel (מְרִיבָה) he asks Lot to avoid.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וּ (‘and’) prefixes the preposition בֵין (‘between’), whose complement is רֹעַי (‘my herders’).
analysis.sense: between (two parties): of covenant, sign, witness, strife

analysis.evidence: Abram pairs רֹעַי “my herdsmen” with רֹעֶיךָ “your herdsmen” as the two groups between whom he wants the quarrel to cease.
analysis.morphology: Qal active participle, masculine plural construct, with a first-person common singular possessive suffix. The participle denotes the people who tend Abram’s livestock.

analysis.evidence: In וּבֵין רֹעַי וּבֵין רֹעֶיךָ ‘between my herdsmen and your herdsmen’, the marked וּבֵין introduces Lot’s herdsmen as the second party to the quarrel (מְרִיבָה) that Abram asks to avoid.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וּ ‘and’ is prefixed to the preposition בֵין ‘between’, whose complement is רֹעֶיךָ ‘your herdsmen’.
analysis.sense: between (two parties): of covenant, sign, witness, strife

analysis.evidence: Abram addresses Lot. The parallel phrases וּבֵין רֹעַי וּבֵין רֹעֶיךָ identify the two groups involved in the quarrel as Abram’s herdsmen (“my herdsmen”) and Lot’s (“your herdsmen”).
analysis.morphology: Qal active participle, masculine plural construct, used as a noun. The second-person masculine singular suffix marks Lot as the possessor.

analysis.evidence: כִּי introduces Abram’s reason for asking Lot to avoid strife between them and between their herdsmen. The clause אֲנָשִׁים אַחִים אֲנָחְנוּ means “we are kinsmen.”
analysis.morphology: Unprefixed Hebrew conjunction with no suffix.

analysis.evidence: Abram includes himself and Lot in אֲנָחְנוּ, “we.” He calls the two of them אֲנָשִׁים, “men,” and אַחִים specifies their relationship, “kinsmen.” Their kinship is his reason for asking that the quarrel cease.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute noun, the irregular plural of אִישׁ, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Abram tells Lot כִּי אֲנָשִׁים אַחִים אֲנָחְנוּ, “for we are kinsmen,” as his reason to avoid strife. Lot is the son of Abram’s brother (Genesis 11:27–31), so אַחִים describes their kinship as uncle and nephew.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine plural, absolute state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Abram tells Lot כִּי אֲנָשִׁים אַחִים אֲנָחְנוּ, “for we are kinsmen.” The final pronoun is the subject of the clause and includes both Abram and Lot.
analysis.morphology: Independent first-person common plural pronoun in pausal form, with no prefix or suffix.
